text.en: Peel an orange and try to lay the peel flat without tearing it. You cannot. This is exactly the problem of drawing the round Earth on a flat map.

The Earth is a nearly spherical shape that bulges at the equator and is slightly flat at the poles, called an oblate spheroid.
A flat map cannot show the round Earth without some distortion, so maps use projections that give a visual idea of size, shape, location and distance.
Physical maps use colours: blue for water bodies, green for plains, and yellow and brown for plateaus and mountains.
Professionals use latitude and longitude coordinates for precise locations.
The ocean is a vast body of salt water covering about 71 per cent of the Earth, which is why the Earth is called the blue planet.
Plankton are microscopic organisms with chlorophyll that make food in the ocean and are the base of marine food chains.
The world has seven continents, each with unique physical features such as mountains, plains, deserts, rivers and plateaus.
Examples of features are the Himalayas in Asia, the Amazon rainforest in South America, the Sahara in Africa and the Antarctic ice sheet.
Human actions such as burning fuels, cutting forests and pollution trigger environmental problems like climate change and habitat loss.
Understanding world geography helps us see how places are connected and how our actions affect distant regions.

problem.en: Why does a flat map distort the Earth?

text.en: The Earth is nearly a sphere.
A curved surface cannot be flattened without stretching or tearing.
So maps use projections that distort some sizes or shapes.

prompt.en: Why do we call Earth the blue planet?

points.en: The Earth is an oblate spheroid; maps use projections.
Human actions cause environmental issues across continents.
